items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists have long assumed that raising the minimum wage pushes employers to cut jobs. However, a growing body of research suggests that the effect may be smaller than predicted. In a study of restaurants on either side of a state border, economist Lena Okafor found that employment in the state that raised its wage grew at nearly the same rate as employment in the neighboring state that did not. Okafor argues that employers often absorb higher wages through lower staff turnover rather than through layoffs.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study confirmed the long-held assumption that higher minimum wages lead employers to cut jobs.
Restaurants in the state that raised its minimum wage saw their employment grow during the study.
Research suggests that raising the minimum wage may reduce employment less than economists have expected.
Raising the minimum wage reliably increases employment because workers leave their jobs less often.
items.explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn in this passage. The old assumption is set up so it can be questioned, and Okafor's border study is the evidence for the newer view. Choice C covers the assumption, the challenge to it and the study, and it keeps the passage's hedge ('may').

A.why: You took the assumption in the first sentence for the conclusion. Okafor's findings challenge that assumption. They don't confirm it.

B.why: You picked a detail from the study that is roughly accurate. It describes one result, but it leaves out the passage's point that this result challenges a long-held assumption.

D.why: You stretched the claim too far. The passage says job losses may be smaller than expected. It never says higher wages reliably increase employment.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Many endurance athletes believe that stretching before a race helps prevent injury. Researchers at a Norwegian sports institute tested this belief by assigning 300 recreational runners to either a stretching routine or a light jogging warm-up for twelve weeks. The two groups reported almost identical numbers of injuries. The researchers concluded that pre-race stretching, though popular, appears to offer little protection against injury.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The runners in the study followed their assigned warm-up routines for a period of twelve weeks.
A study found that stretching before running does little to prevent injury, despite a common belief.
Light jogging is the most effective warm-up for runners who want to avoid injury before a race.
Most endurance athletes have stopped stretching before races because they doubt it prevents injury.
items.explanation: The last sentence sums up the passage: stretching before a race, though popular, offers little protection against injury. Choice B covers both the common belief and the study's finding that undercuts it.

A.why: You chose a true detail about how the study was set up. The length of the study isn't what the passage is trying to show.

C.why: You went beyond the evidence. The two groups had about the same number of injuries, so the study doesn't show that jogging works better than stretching, let alone that it's the most effective warm-up.

D.why: You reversed what the passage says about athletes. It says many of them believe stretching prevents injury, not that they have stopped doing it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, archaeologists credited the stone terraces at a hillside site in the Andes to the Inca, who controlled the region in the fifteenth century. However, recent radiocarbon dating of charcoal buried beneath the lowest terrace walls indicates that the terraces were built roughly three hundred years before the Inca arrived. The findings suggest that an earlier, less well-documented community was responsible for the construction.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Inca controlled the Andean region where the stone terraces are found during the fifteenth century.
Radiocarbon dating shows that the Inca borrowed their farming methods from earlier Andean communities.
Recent evidence confirms that the Inca built the terraces soon after they arrived in the region.
New dating evidence suggests that the terraces were built by a community that predated the Inca.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the old view that the Inca built the terraces, then turns with 'However' to the dating evidence. What comes after the turn is the author's point: an earlier community probably built them. Choice D says this and keeps the hedge ('suggests').

A.why: You picked background from the first sentence. It's accurate, but the passage mentions it only to set up the older view that the new evidence corrects.

B.why: You added a claim the passage never makes. The dating shows when the terraces were built, not whether the Inca borrowed anyone's farming methods.

C.why: You stopped at the older view. The dating places the terraces about three hundred years before the Inca arrived, so it undercuts that view.

items.stimulus: Engineers are increasingly using recycled materials to make road surfaces more durable. For example, a team in the Netherlands mixed shredded plastic waste into the asphalt of a two-kilometer test road. After three years of heavy truck traffic, the plastic-blend section showed about half as many cracks as a conventional section laid at the same time, and it cost no more to build.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Recycled materials can help make road surfaces more durable, as one Dutch test road illustrates.
Shredded plastic is now the standard ingredient in asphalt roads throughout the Netherlands.
The Dutch test road was two kilometers long and carried heavy truck traffic for three years.
Roads made with recycled plastic cracked more often than conventional roads but cost less to build.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim, and 'For example' brings in a single case that supports it. Choice A covers both the claim and the test road that illustrates it.

B.why: You turned one test road into a nationwide standard. The passage describes a single experiment, not a common practice.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fermented foods such as yogurt and kimchi contain live bacteria, and some researchers have proposed that eating them may strengthen the immune system. In a small trial, adults who ate several servings of fermented foods daily for ten weeks showed lower levels of certain inflammation markers than adults who did not. The researchers caution, however, that the trial was brief and that larger studies are needed before such foods can be recommended for immune health.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Yogurt and kimchi are among the fermented foods that researchers say contain live bacteria.
Eating fermented foods daily has been proven to protect adults from illnesses linked to inflammation.
A small trial offers early support for fermented foods aiding immunity, but more research is needed.
The trial found that fermented foods had no measurable effect on the inflammation levels of adults.
items.explanation: The hedge words ('may', 'small', 'brief', 'larger studies are needed') limit how strong the claim can be. The passage reports a promising result and then warns that it isn't conclusive. Choice C includes both the promise and the warning.

A.why: You picked a background fact from the first sentence. It names the foods but says nothing about the trial or the researchers' caution.

B.why: You ignored the hedges. The researchers say more studies are needed, so nothing has been 'proven', and the trial measured inflammation markers, not illnesses.

D.why: You reversed the result. Adults who ate fermented foods had lower levels of some inflammation markers, which is a measurable effect.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have long assumed that innate immune cells such as macrophages, unlike T cells and B cells, keep no memory of past infections. Recent work suggests that this view is incomplete. In a study led by immunologist Rafaela Okonjo, mice whose macrophages had been exposed to a harmless fungal compound responded more quickly to an unrelated bacterial infection weeks later. The macrophages appeared to keep a kind of readiness from their earlier encounter, an effect researchers now call "trained immunity."
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okonjo's study found that macrophages lose any readiness from an earlier encounter within a few weeks.
Research suggests that innate immune cells may keep a form of memory, which challenges a long-held assumption.
In Okonjo's study, the macrophages of mice were exposed to a harmless compound taken from a fungus.
Trained immunity makes innate immune cells just as effective as T cells and B cells at fighting infections.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an old assumption (innate cells have no memory), says it is incomplete, and then gives Okonjo's study as evidence that macrophages can keep a kind of readiness. Choice B covers both parts: the evidence and the assumption it challenges. Its hedge ('suggests', 'may') matches the passage's 'suggests' and 'appeared to'.

A.why: You reversed the finding. The macrophages responded more quickly weeks later, so they kept their readiness rather than losing it.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it only describes how the study was set up. It leaves out what the study found and why that finding matters, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

D.why: The passage never compares how effective innate cells are with T cells and B cells. You stretched 'a kind of readiness' into a much bigger claim than the text supports.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The fiddle tunes of the Ardel Valley have usually been described as a purely local tradition, handed down from player to player within the valley for generations. However, musicologist Tomas Brenner has found that several of the region's best-known melodies closely match dance tunes printed in a 1790s songbook from a port city two hundred miles away. Brenner argues that the valley's music, though shaped by local players, likely drew in part on printed sources from beyond the region.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Ardel Valley's fiddle tradition developed entirely within the valley, without any outside influence.
A songbook printed in a distant port city during the 1790s included a number of popular dance tunes.
Most folk music traditions that seem local actually began as tunes printed in city songbooks.
Evidence suggests that the Ardel Valley's fiddle tunes likely drew in part on music from outside the region.
items.explanation: The word 'However' signals the real point. The passage first gives the usual view that the tradition is purely local, then presents Brenner's evidence and conclusion that the tunes likely drew in part on outside printed sources. Choice D states that conclusion with the same level of caution as the passage ('likely', 'in part').

A.why: This is the view the passage sets up only to correct. Everything after 'However' argues against it, so you chose the opposite of the author's point.

B.why: The songbook is one piece of evidence, not the point it supports. This choice never mentions the Ardel Valley tunes or Brenner's conclusion, so it is too narrow.

C.why: The passage discusses only one region's tunes. You stretched one case into a claim about most folk traditions, and the text never makes that claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the 1850s, surveyor Ines Calloway set out to map the Merrow River delta, a maze of channels that changed shape from year to year. She measured channel depths by hand, recorded which channels shifted after floods, and asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons. Because she documented how the delta moved rather than fixing it at a single moment, her map stayed useful to navigators for decades after other maps of the delta had gone out of date.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Calloway's map stayed useful for decades because it recorded how the delta changed over time.
Calloway asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons.
Calloway's methods became the standard for mapmakers of river deltas around the world.
Calloway's map soon went out of date because the delta's channels shifted after floods.
items.explanation: The middle sentence lists Calloway's methods, and the last sentence sums them up: because she recorded how the delta moved, her map stayed useful for decades. Choice A states that verdict and the reason for it, so it covers the whole passage.

B.why: This is true, but it is only one of the three methods in the middle sentence. It leaves out the result the passage builds toward, so it is too narrow.

C.why: The passage says only that her map stayed useful to navigators of this one delta. It never says that other mapmakers anywhere adopted her methods.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. Other maps went out of date, but Calloway's stayed useful because she accounted for the shifting channels.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Linguists have long observed that words people use often tend to grow shorter over time. A study by linguist Mireille Danso offers a clear case. Danso recorded fish sellers in a coastal market who name one particular species dozens of times each day. These sellers used a clipped, two-syllable form of its name, whereas residents of inland villages, who rarely mention the fish, still used the full five-syllable word.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Residents of inland villages use a long name for a fish that coastal sellers call by a much shorter name.
Danso's study suggests that the words speakers rarely use are the ones most likely to become shorter.
Danso's study gives an example of how using a word frequently can lead speakers to shorten it.
Danso's study shows that coastal speakers shorten nearly all of their words more than inland speakers do.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim: words used often tend to get shorter. Everything after it is one example, introduced as 'a clear case.' The sellers say the fish's name constantly and use a short form, and the villagers rarely say it and keep the long form. Choice C covers both the general claim and the study that supports it, and it doesn't claim more than the text does.

A.why: This is accurate, but it only repeats the contrast from the last sentence. It leaves out the claim that the contrast supports, which is that frequent use leads to shortening. You picked a true detail instead of the point of the whole passage.

B.why: This gets the relationship backward. In the text, the rarely used name stays long and the frequently used one gets shorter. You may have recognized 'Danso's study' and 'shorter' and stopped reading before the claim turned wrong.

D.why: The study looks at one fish name. It says nothing about coastal speakers shortening 'nearly all' their words. You stretched a single example into a broad claim about how two groups speak.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, engineers designing pedestrian bridges in the city of Varn concentrated on the strength of the main beams, assuming those beams would need the most repair over a bridge's life. However, a 2019 survey of the city's forty footbridges found that most repairs had involved something else: the small joints that let each bridge's deck expand in summer heat. Inspectors now check these joints first.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A survey confirmed that the main beams were the footbridge parts that most often needed repair, as engineers expected.
A survey revealed that expansion joints, rather than main beams, were the footbridge parts most often needing repair.
Footbridge decks in Varn expand during summer heat, so they are built with small joints that allow them to move.
A survey showed that expansion joints cause most of the repairs needed by bridges of every type around the world.
items.explanation: The passage first describes what engineers expected: the main beams would need the most repair. Then 'However' introduces what the survey actually found, which was that the expansion joints needed most of the repairs. The final sentence describes what changed as a result. Choice B states this correction, and it stays within the forty footbridges that were surveyed.

A.why: This repeats the engineers' old assumption as if the survey had confirmed it. The word 'However' signals that the survey found the opposite. You read the setup and missed the turn.

C.why: The text does say the joints let the deck expand in heat, but that's only background to explain what the joints are. It doesn't mention the expectation, the survey, or the finding. You chose a true detail instead of the main point.

D.why: The survey covered forty footbridges in one city. Nothing in the text supports a claim about 'bridges of every type around the world.' You started with the right finding and then stretched it far beyond the evidence.

items.stimulus: Many cities are replacing parking spaces with small public seating areas. In one riverside neighborhood, planners converted twelve curbside spaces into benches and planters. Within a year, nearby cafés reported more customers, and residents said the street felt safer at night. Turning some parking into seating can make a street more useful to people.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds to every threat as if meeting it for the first time. choices: Halloway argues that the barley from the storage pit is younger than 7000 BCE and so cannot show early farming at Tel Varon.
Halloway argues that the residents of Tel Varon gathered their barley from wild stands rather than farming it around 7000 BCE.
Halloway notes that the barley grains from the pit are small and lack the stalk joint typical of domesticated barley.
Halloway accepts the early date of the barley but argues that it does not by itself show the grain was farmed at that time.
items.explanation: Halloway makes a limited concession (the date is right) and then an objection (the grains do not prove farming). Her hedges set how strong the claim is: the grains 'could' be wild, and cultivation is 'possible'. Choice D keeps both halves and matches that level of certainty.

B.why: You noticed that Halloway is skeptical, but you missed her hedges. She says the grains 'could easily' be wild and that farming is 'possible'. She does not say the residents did not farm. This choice turns 'not proven' into 'disproven'.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Studies of the etcher Henrik Saal usually treat the faint gray tone in his skies as the result of careless wiping of the plate. Conservator Lena Achterberg examined forty impressions of his 1871 harbor view and found the tone in the same position in every one. She also located a notebook entry in which Saal describes a tool for leaving a thin film of ink on chosen areas, and she observed that the tone appears only in prints Saal pulled himself, not in later editions printed by others. Taken together, Achterberg argues, the evidence indicates the tone was deliberate.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Achterberg found that the gray tone appears in the same position in all forty impressions of Saal's 1871 harbor view that she examined.
Achterberg combines several kinds of evidence to argue that a tone usually seen as accidental in Saal's skies was in fact intended.
Achterberg's examination confirms the usual view that the gray tone in Saal's skies resulted from his wiping the plate unevenly.
Achterberg argues that Saal intended the gray tone in his skies, so the later editions printed by others misrepresent his work.
items.explanation: The middle sentences list three separate findings: the tone is in the same place every time, there is a notebook entry, and the tone appears only in Saal's own printings. The last sentence combines them into one verdict that overturns the usual view. Choice B covers both the combining and the verdict.

A.why: This is accurate, but it is only one of the three findings. It leaves out the conclusion they support. This is the vivid-detail trap: true, and too narrow.

C.why: This turns the passage around. The careless-wiping explanation is the view Achterberg argues against, not one she confirms.

D.why: The first half matches her conclusion. The second half adds a judgment she never makes. The passage uses the later editions only as evidence. It never says they misrepresent Saal. Read every choice to the end.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Planners often assume that new bike lanes draw their riders mainly from people who previously drove. A 2022 study of the city of Velmora suggests a more complicated picture. After the city opened twelve kilometers of protected lanes, cycling on the affected streets rose by 40 percent. But surveys of the new riders found that most had previously taken the bus or walked, and car traffic on parallel routes was essentially unchanged.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Velmora study shows that protected bike lanes can increase cycling but cannot reduce car traffic in any city that builds them.
After Velmora opened twelve kilometers of protected bike lanes, cycling on the affected streets increased by about 40 percent.
The Velmora study suggests that new bike lanes may increase cycling without drawing many of their new riders away from cars.
The Velmora study suggests that new bike lanes draw riders away from buses, which planners should count as a cost of the lanes.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an assumption and then tests it with one case. The 'But' sentence is the finding: cycling rose, but the new riders mostly came from buses and walking, and car traffic stayed the same. Choice C covers both the rise and where the riders came from. Its 'suggests' and 'may' match the passage's 'suggests a more complicated picture'.

A.why: One city's study cannot support 'cannot' and 'any city'. You got the direction right and then made it absolute.

B.why: This is the 40 percent figure, which is accurate and easy to remember. But it leaves out the 'But' sentence, and that sentence is what makes the picture 'more complicated'.

D.why: The first half is supported: most new riders came from buses or walking. The second half adds a policy judgment that the passage never makes. Nothing in the text calls the shift a cost.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Hydrologists estimating how much water a watershed can supply have traditionally relied on rain and stream gauges. Priya Ndlovu and colleagues compared such estimates for the Kessel Basin with measurements from satellites that detect changes in the mass of water stored underground. The gauges had indicated that the basin's supply was stable from 2005 to 2020, but the satellite data showed groundwater declining steadily over the same period, a loss the gauges, which record only surface flows, were never designed to detect.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ndlovu's team found that the Kessel Basin was losing groundwater that gauge-based estimates, limited to surface water, had missed.
Ndlovu's team found that the Kessel Basin's gauges had been malfunctioning, which made the basin's water supply appear stable.
Ndlovu's team found that satellites should replace rain and stream gauges as hydrologists' main tool for estimating water supply.
Ndlovu's team found that gauge-based estimates indicated the Kessel Basin's water supply remained stable from 2005 to 2020.
items.explanation: The passage builds to the 'but' clause: the satellites showed a groundwater loss that the gauges could not record, because the gauges measure only surface flow. Choice A gives the finding and the reason the gauges missed it. It also stays inside the one basin that was studied.

B.why: You saw that the gauges got the answer wrong and assumed they were broken. The passage says they were 'never designed to detect' groundwater. The gauges worked as intended. They just measure something else.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap: it treats a new tool as doing more than the passage describes. The study found one gap in one basin. It never says satellites should replace gauges.

D.why: This is true, but it is the expected view the passage sets up before the 'but'. It leaves out what the satellites showed.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Intercropping, or growing two crops in the same field, has been promoted as a way to cut fertilizer use, because legumes such as beans add nitrogen to the soil. In a three-year trial in Tamsey County, agronomist Felix Brannigan found that maize grown alongside beans needed about a quarter less nitrogen fertilizer than maize grown alone, with no loss in yield. Brannigan cautions, however, that the trial years brought unusually heavy rainfall, which favors bean growth, and that savings in drier years are likely to be smaller.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Brannigan's trial shows that intercropping maize with beans cuts fertilizer needs by about a quarter, whatever the rainfall.
Brannigan's trial found that maize grown alongside beans produced as large a harvest as maize grown on its own.
Brannigan's trial suggests that intercropping is unlikely to reduce fertilizer use at all in years with ordinary rainfall.
Brannigan's trial supports the fertilizer savings of intercropping, but he expects those savings to shrink in drier years.
items.explanation: The trial supports the claim made at the start, and then 'however' limits it: the wet years probably made the savings look bigger. 'Likely to be smaller' is the hedge you need to keep. Choice D keeps both the support and the limit, at the same strength the passage uses.

A.why: This repeats the trial's result and drops the 'however'. 'Whatever the rainfall' is the opposite of Brannigan's warning that rainfall probably increased the savings.

B.why: 'No loss in yield' is in the passage, but it is a side detail of the trial. This choice says nothing about fertilizer or about Brannigan's warning.

C.why: You caught the warning and then made it too strong. Brannigan says savings in drier years are 'likely to be smaller', not that they disappear. Going from 'smaller' to 'none at all' goes past the hedge.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Forecasters have generally credited the improved accuracy of five-day hurricane track forecasts since the 1990s to faster supercomputers that run models at finer resolution. Meteorologist Celia Varga tested this by rerunning older forecast models on modern computers. The reruns improved only modestly; most of the gain appeared only when the models were also fed today's denser observations from aircraft and satellites. Varga does not dismiss computing power, but she concludes that better data has done more of the work than is usually acknowledged.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Varga's analysis shows that faster supercomputers have done little to improve five-day hurricane track forecasts since the 1990s.
Varga's analysis indicates that denser observations account for more of the gain in track forecasts than faster computing does.
Varga's analysis shows that older forecast models improve only modestly when they are rerun on modern computers.
Varga's analysis indicates that forecasts of all kinds now depend more on observational data than on computing power.
items.explanation: The passage gives the usual credit, a test of it, and a conclusion after 'but'. That conclusion is that data did more of the work than computing, and Varga 'does not dismiss computing power'. Choice B is a comparison ('more of the gain'), which matches her conclusion. It does not drop computing, and it stays with hurricane track forecasts.

A.why: You saw that data mattered more and assumed computing mattered very little. The reruns did improve, modestly, and Varga explicitly does not dismiss computing power. 'Done little' contradicts that.

C.why: This is the result of one step in Varga's test. It leaves out the observations, and they are the point of her conclusion. It is too narrow.

D.why: Varga studied five-day hurricane track forecasts. This choice stretches her finding to 'forecasts of all kinds', which the passage never claims.
